content: 1. Tuberculosis (TB) is a significant cause of hospitalization and in-hospital mortality among individuals living with HIV worldwide, as demonstrated by systematic reviews and meta-analyses. These studies highlight the global burden of TB in this population and emphasize the need for effective prevention and management strategies. 2. Severe bacterial infections unrelated to TB are common in HIV-infected adults. Expert reviews have outlined management strategies for these infections, emphasizing the importance of timely diagnosis and appropriate anti-infective therapy. 3. Hospital admissions among people living with HIV are often due to opportunistic infections, including TB and cryptococcal meningitis. Systematic reviews have identified the primary causes of these admissions, providing insights into global trends and regional variations. 4. HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis remains a major contributor to morbidity and mortality worldwide. Updated analyses of its global burden underscore the need for improved diagnostic and therapeutic approaches. 5. Histoplasmosis, a fungal infection, is increasingly recognized as a global health concern, particularly in regions outside the Ohio River Valley. Studies have highlighted its prevalence among people with advanced HIV and its co-occurrence with TB. 6. Toxoplasma gondii infection is prevalent among HIV-infected individuals, with systematic reviews quantifying its global burden. This highlights the importance of screening and prophylaxis in this population. 7. Penicillium marneffei infection, an emerging fungal disease, has been studied extensively in Southeast Asia and China. Research has identified its epidemiology, seasonality, and predictors of outcomes, emphasizing the need for heightened awareness in endemic regions. 8. The emergence of new dimorphic fungal pathogens, such as Emergomyces, has been documented globally. These pathogens pose a growing threat to immunocompromised individuals, including those with HIV. 9. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis is a significant HIV-related complication in resource-limited settings. Systematic reviews have assessed its burden and highlighted the need for improved access to diagnostic and treatment options. 10. Point-of-care CD4 testing has been shown to enhance linkage to HIV care and expedite antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses support its integration into public health approaches. 11. Cryptococcal meningitis screening and early adherence support for individuals with advanced HIV starting ART have been evaluated in randomized controlled trials. These interventions have demonstrated improved outcomes in resource-limited settings. 12. Enhanced prophylaxis combined with ART has been shown to reduce mortality in individuals with advanced HIV in Africa. This approach includes interventions targeting opportunistic infections such as TB and cryptococcal meningitis. 13. WHO guidelines on TB prevention, screening, and rapid diagnostics provide comprehensive recommendations for managing TB in people living with HIV. These guidelines emphasize the importance of systematic screening and preventive treatment. 14. Cryptococcal immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) is a significant cause of early mortality in HIV programs. Studies have proposed clinical case definitions and management strategies for this condition. 15. Early initiation of ART in individuals with HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis has been evaluated in clinical trials. Findings suggest that timing of ART initiation is critical to optimizing outcomes. 16. Amphotericin B-based induction therapy for cryptococcal meningitis is associated with significant toxicity. Studies have explored strategies to mitigate renal toxicity, including standardized electrolyte supplementation and fluid management. 17. Disseminated histoplasmosis is a common opportunistic infection in individuals with AIDS. Clinical guidelines recommend liposomal amphotericin B as a safe and effective induction therapy, followed by itraconazole for maintenance. 18. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is recommended for individuals with advanced HIV to prevent opportunistic infections, including bacterial infections and malaria. Guidelines provide criteria for initiation and discontinuation based on clinical and immunological status. 19. Physical activity is associated with numerous health benefits for individuals living with HIV, including improved cardiovascular health, mental well-being, and reduced mortality. WHO guidelines recommend regular physical activity tailored to age and health status. 20. Comprehensive HIV care includes combination prevention, ART, and management of coinfections and comorbidities. WHO guidelines outline a package of interventions to improve quality of life and reduce HIV transmission. 21. Research gaps remain in understanding the health effects of physical activity and sedentary behavior in underserved populations. Further studies are needed to refine recommendations and address disparities in evidence availability. 22. General care for people living with HIV should include psychosocial support, TB screening, fungal infection prevention, and vaccination. These interventions aim to reduce morbidity and improve overall health outcomes. 23. WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of integrating HIV prevention, testing, treatment, and care services into national health policies. This approach aims to achieve universal access and improve health outcomes for people living with HIV.
